source.title: DeSteer: Adaptive Defense Against LLM Jailbreak Attacks via Intent-Conditioned Latent Vector Steering

page_placements.theme: Safety steering by adding refusal or safety vectors at inference: gains, over-refusal and capability costs, gating

record.file_problem: The text includes flattened table formatting and some missing names in prose. It is not cut off; the per-cell mapping in Table 1 is not secure enough to extract.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses latent representation steering to build a jailbreak defense, but reports only the performance of its own intent-conditioned, learned refusal-vector method. It does not test the original difference-in-means direction or whether that direction mediates refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper describes DeSteer as representation engineering and cites contrastive concept-difference methods, but its refusal vectors are learned to produce successive refusal tokens; it does not report results for a harmful-minus-harmless mean direction. The detector's token-window results are used to select k=1, so they are not recorded as rows. Per-cell results from Table 1 are omitted because the flattened layout does not securely assign all values to models and metrics; explicit aggregate statements are recorded instead. Results about other baselines are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: DeSteer is a jailbreak defense. It trains an MLP intent detector and a set of per-token refusal vectors, each optimized by cross-entropy to emit fixed refusal tokens ('Sorry', ',', 'but', ...). These are added at the final layer for the first N decoding steps. No harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction is computed, ablated or added. All reported results are the defense's own performance against baselines (ASR, HS, MT-Bench, GSM8K, XSTest). Nothing tests whether a single direction mediates refusal, whether attacks suppress it, or any other version. Induced refusal here comes from vectors trained to output refusal tokens, which is inducing the behaviour on purpose.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Authors conclude DeSteer achieves SOTA jailbreak defense without compromising utility. The false-refusal cost on Vicuna appears in their Limitations, not the conclusion itself.
record.recipe_differences: DeSteer uses a trained intent-detection head and a token-indexed set of learned refusal vectors, optimized on harmful prompts and injected at the final layer for the first N generation steps according to a risk score. It does not calculate or ablate a single harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with steering duration N, steering intensity p, and model; the paper states Vicuna needs stronger steering and incurs higher false-refusal rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Intent-conditioned, learned per-token refusal vectors added at the final layer for the first N steps cut jailbreak ASR to at most 5% on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, Vicuna-7B and Falcon-7B-Instruct.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Risk-scaled additive steering with optimized refusal vectors reduces jailbreak success at modest utility cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Utility and false-refusal cost of the steering varies by model. Vicuna XSTest false refusal rises from 8% to 43%; LLaMA-2 stays at 24%. MT-Bench drops by about 10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Costs of additive refusal steering depend on the model's intrinsic alignment strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Defense strength depends on the number of steered steps N and on intensity p.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-vector steering effect scales with steering duration and magnitude.

record.problems: The paper evaluates DeSteer rather than the claimed difference-in-means direction, so its results do not test the claim versions directly. The paper focuses on 7B models and single-turn text-only prompts; it identifies possible out-of-distribution detector failures and higher false-refusal costs on Vicuna. The Table 1 extraction is flattened, and no uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Per-attack Table 1 values for LLaMA-2 and Vicuna were left out because the flattened table layout does not securely establish cell-to-model and cell-to-metric assignments. The token-window detector figures in Figure 3 were used to select k=1 and are not intervention outcomes. Other defense baselines are not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Difference-in-means direction; its ablation removing refusal; its addition inducing refusal; capability preservation under ablation.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction; adversarial training against ablation. The study defends against jailbreaks but never measures the direction under attack.
Single vs multi-direction or cone or affine structure. The learned per-token vector set is a design choice, not compared with a single direction.
Separate harm vs refusal encoding. The detector reads harmfulness from the final hidden state, but its relation to a refusal direction is not tested.
Transfer across languages, models, or base-to-instruct. Falcon results retrain DeSteer per model; no transfer of a direction is tested.
Effect of refusal training method or timing.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 is readable enough: rows are defenses and columns are HEx-PHI, DeepInception, ReNeLLM, AmpleGCG, ICA, AutoDAN-T and RS. The column order in the flattened text is uncertain, though, so leaving per-cell rows out is defensible. None of the rows bear on any version, so no verdicts are given. The paper cites CAA and ActAdd but not Arditi et al.

versions.untested_parts: The single harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, its removal at every layer and position, and its addition without risk conditioning.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separate representation of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
Falcon is evaluated with DeSteer, but transfer of the claimed difference-in-means direction across models, languages, or training stages is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or timing for the existence of a removable direction is reported.

relation.reason: Learned refusal steering vectors are the paper's tool. It runs no test of whether one difference-in-means direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: The paper uses learned 'token-level refusal directions' as a defense tool and reports only its own performance. It is borderline with T6: the vectors are CE-optimized per token and added to the final hidden state before the LM head. They are not a harmful-minus-harmless direction, and Arditi et al. are not cited.

source_check.notes: The refusal vectors are added only to the final-layer state just before the LM head, so in effect they act as a per-step logit bias scaled by p, not a residual-stream direction. Table 1 is flattened. By column order (HEx-PHI, DeepInception, ReNeLLM, AmpleGCG, ICA, AutoDAN-T, RS), the Vicuna 65% no-defense cell is probably ICA, not RS as the r2 verdict fix says. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is right.

statements.correction: MT-Bench No Defense to DeSteer: LLaMA-2 4.68 to 4.24 (-9.4%), Vicuna 4.74 to 4.23 (-10.8%), Falcon-7B-Instruct 3.00 to 2.42 (-19%). Max DeSteer ASR: LLaMA-2 3%, Vicuna 4%, Falcon 5%.
statements.problem: Every number is in the text. But 'MT-Bench drops by about 10%' holds only for LLaMA-2 and Vicuna. The sentence names three models, and Falcon-7B-Instruct dropped about 19%.
